title: Setup words
teaches: The names on our setup list and what each one means: the Kicker, Oops Reversal, Slingshot, Launchpad, High Volume Edge (HVC), Gap Support and the Go Signal, the catalog family each sits in, the Bear gap lesson, and the plan words every setup carries: trigger, stop, R, the first sell as a judgment (usually day 3 or later), the stop to breakeven, partials, trail.

walkthroughs.title: Every setup carries a plan
steps: Every trade plan we teach hands you two prices: the trigger, which is the entry, and the stop.
R is your risk per share, entry to stop. The first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later.
Then you trail. The stop follows the stock up, under each higher low or a rising average.

walkthroughs.title: Names and families
steps: Our catalog sorts every setup into a family. Learn the family and the name gets easier to place.
The Kicker, High Volume Edge and Gap Support are Gaps & Catalysts. Oops Reversal and Slingshot are Reversals & Reclaims.
The Launchpad sits in Bases & Breakouts. The Go Signal and the ORB are Intraday.

walkthroughs.title: A name is not an edge
steps: The textbook kicker is a down candle, then a gap up the other way.
Investopedia calls it highly reliable. Bulkowski's tests found it reversed the trend 53% of the time, almost random.
So I don't trade the name. I trade the plan: our entry, our stop, a first sell by judgment.

questions.q: In our setup plans, what is a setup's trigger?
questions.why: The setup's entry price. In our plans, trigger means entry. Each setup's detector returns its own trigger and its own stop for the candle it fires on. The trigger is a price on the chart. It is not the stop, not a profit target, and not the news behind the move. Selling comes later, and the first sell is a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Trigger means entry. Every setup hands you one, plus a stop.

wrong.The setup's stop price: The stop is the other price each setup gives you. The trigger is where you get in.
wrong.The first target: Selling comes later, and the first sell is a judgment, not a fixed target.
wrong.The news that moved it: News can be why a stock moves. The trigger is a price on the chart.

questions.simple: The trigger is the entry price, the spot where you get in, and each setup gives you one along with a stop.

reasons: wrong note rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.why: Trim. Our plans run Entry, Stop, Trim, Trail: get in, set the stop, take some off, then trail the rest. Our full line ends with Advance. The first sell is a judgment, rarely on day 1, and the last part trails.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, Stop, Trim, Trail. Every trade plan we teach runs in that order.
questions.simple: Trim comes third because you take some profit off as the trade works, then trail the rest.

questions.q: In candle terms, what is a bullish kicker?
choices: A red candle, then a gap-up green one
A green candle, then a gap-down red one
One candle with a long lower wick
A small candle inside the prior range
questions.answer: A red candle, then a gap-up green one
questions.why: A red candle, then a gap-up green one. Investopedia: bullish kickers start with a bearish candle and then show a bullish gap up. Bulkowski's version is stricter: a tall black marubozu, an upward gap, then a tall white marubozu. The mirror image, a green candle then a gap-down red one, is the bearish kicker. One candle alone is never a kicker.
questions.lesson_line: Kicker: a down day, then a gap up going the other way.

wrong.A green candle, then a gap-down red one: That's the bearish kicker, the mirror image.
wrong.One candle with a long lower wick: One candle can't be a kicker. It takes two candles with a gap between them.
wrong.A small candle inside the prior range: A candle inside the day before has no gap. A kicker gaps away from the day before.

questions.simple: A bullish kicker is a red candle, then a green candle that gaps up, a sharp flip from down to up.

reasons: two Tier 2 publishers agree; stable definition

questions.q: In our setup list, what is an Oops Reversal?
choices: A gap up the day after a red day
A move back over a 4-day high average
A move out of a tight MA cluster
questions.why: The prior close, reclaimed intraday. The stock trades under yesterday's close, then gets back over it during the day. That reclaim is the entry. The plan then sells in parts, the first sell a judgment, and trails under each higher low. It is not the Kicker, which gaps up after a red day.
questions.lesson_line: Oops: it lost the prior close and took it back the same day.

wrong.A gap up the day after a red day: That's the Kicker: a red day, then a gap up the next day.
wrong.A move back over a 4-day high average: That's the Slingshot's entry: price trading back over the 4-day average of the highs.

questions.simple: An Oops Reversal is a stock that drops under yesterday's close and then climbs back over it the same day.

reasons: house definition from TRADE_PLANS.md; stable

questions.q: What is a Launchpad in our setup list?
choices: A break out of a tight MA cluster
A move back over a 4-day high average
A pullback that holds an old gap
A weak open that buyers turn up
questions.answer: A break out of a tight MA cluster
questions.why: A break out of a tight MA cluster. The moving averages squeeze together, and we buy as price trades out of the cluster, never at the close. The line-based stop sits under the 20 EMA and 50 SMA, a quarter of an ATR below the lower one. It is not the Slingshot, whose line is the 4-day average of the highs.
questions.lesson_line: Launchpad: averages squeezed together, then price breaks out of the squeeze.

wrong.A pullback that holds an old gap: That's Gap Support, a pullback that holds an old gap.
wrong.A move back over a 4-day high average: That's the Slingshot. Its line is a short average of the highs, not a cluster.

questions.simple: A Launchpad is when the moving averages bunch up tight and price then breaks out of that bunch.

reasons: house definition from TRADE_PLANS.md; stable

questions.q: What is Gap Support in our setup list?
choices: Buying a pullback that holds a gap
Shorting a gap down off the highs
Buying the open of any gap up
Waiting for a gap to fill, then buying
questions.answer: Buying a pullback that holds a gap
questions.why: Buying a pullback that holds a gap. The stock gaps up and runs, then comes back to the gap and holds. We buy as price trades up through the trigger while the gap holds, never at the close. The stop is the gap top or the day's low, whichever is lower. If it drifts sideways at the gap, the stop tightens to just under the gap top. It is not buying the open of a fresh gap, and it does not wait for the gap to fill.
questions.lesson_line: Gap Support: the gap holds, you buy, and the gap is your line.

wrong.Shorting a gap down off the highs: Gap Support buys. A short off a gap down is the Bear gap lesson, and that one is measured, not traded.
wrong.Buying the open of any gap up: Gap Support waits for the gap to prove it holds. The buy comes later, as price trades up through its trigger.
wrong.Waiting for a gap to fill, then buying: We buy while the gap still holds, not after it fills.

questions.simple: Gap Support means buying when a stock pulls back to an old gap and the gap holds.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: Our catalog lists HVC with the High Volume Edge. What is the HVC?
choices: The close of a high-volume day
The highest price of the day
A high-volume gap at the open
questions.answer: The close of a high-volume day
questions.why: The close of a high-volume day. Our catalog files HVC with the High Volume Edge, and the HVC is the price where the heavy day closed. We mark it as a level, and we buy as price trades through the trigger, never at the close. It is not a volume reading, a gap, or the day's high.
questions.lesson_line: High Volume Edge: the HVC is where the heavy-volume day closed, a level we mark.

wrong.The highest price of the day: That's the high. The HVC is the close of the heavy-volume day.
wrong.A high-volume gap at the open: It isn't about a gap. The HVC is where the heavy-volume day closed.
wrong.Volume above its 50-day average: That's a volume reading, not a price. The HVC is the close of that heavy day.

questions.simple: The HVC is the close of the heavy-volume day, not its high or a volume reading.

reasons: the HVC expansion has no citable house quote (owner flag)

questions.q: What is our Go Signal?
choices: A weak open that buyers turn back up
A gap up the day after a red day
A pullback that holds an older gap up
A break out of a tight MA cluster
questions.answer: A weak open that buyers turn back up
questions.why: A weak open that buyers turn back up. It is an intraday entry in a stock that has already shown it can move. The day opens under the prior close. The low sweeps a nearby support. Then buyers step in and turn it.
questions.lesson_line: Go Signal: a strong stock opens weak, flushes support, and buyers turn it.

wrong.A gap up the day after a red day: That's the Kicker: a red day, then a gap up the next day.
wrong.A pullback that holds an older gap up: That's Gap Support, a pullback that holds an older gap.

questions.simple: The Go Signal is a strong stock that opens weak, dips through support, and then buyers turn it back up.

reasons: house definition from TRADE_PLANS.md; stable

The Launchpad breaks out of a cluster of averages. The Oops takes back the prior close during the day. The Go Signal turns a weak open back up intraday.
questions.lesson_line: Slingshot: back over the 4-day average of the highs, as price trades through it.

wrong.Launchpad: The Launchpad breaks out of a tight cluster of averages.
wrong.Oops Reversal: The Oops reclaims the prior close during the day.
wrong.Go Signal: The Go Signal turns a weak open back up during the day.

questions.story: You buy a setup at $60 with its stop at $57. It reaches $69 and keeps going.
questions.q: Counting in R, where is it?
questions.why: At 3R. Your risk is the gap from the $60 entry down to the $57 stop. The gain to $69 is three times that risk. 3R is a mark to measure with, not an order to sell. R counts from the entry, not from the stop, and it is never the dollar gain itself.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R: the gain divided by your entry-to-stop risk.

wrong.At 9R: nine dollars: That's dollars, not R. Divide the gain by your risk per share.
wrong.At 4R: from the stop: That counts from the $57 stop. R counts the gain from your $60 entry, in units of your risk.
wrong.At 5R, five times the risk: 5R needs five times the risk. This is three.

questions.simple: At 3R, because the gain from $60 to $69 is three times your risk from $60 to $57.

deeper.example: Same trade, keep going. 5R is five times your risk per share, added to the $60 entry. These are marks to measure with. The first sell is a judgment, rarely on day 1, and the last part trails under the rising averages.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: Why does a huge-volume day's close become a level worth watching?
choices: Heavy volume usually marks a top
Volume shows the next day's direction
Big volume means it was all buying
questions.why: Big volume usually means institutions. IBD says large increases in trading volume are usually the work of institutions, buying or selling. Investopedia says the big traders create big volume. That is why our High Volume Edge treats the high-volume close, the HVC, as a level. The first return to it is the cleanest decision point. Volume does not say which way, and it does not call a top.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume leaves a footprint. The close of that day is a level.

wrong.Heavy volume usually marks a top: Not usually. Investopedia says breakouts on high volume are more likely to keep going.
wrong.Volume shows the next day's direction: Volume shows who was active, not what tomorrow does.
wrong.Big volume means it was all buying: Volume counts both sides. IBD says big jumps in volume are usually institutions buying or selling.

questions.simple: Big volume usually means institutions were trading, so the close of that day is a price worth watching.

deeper.counter: Volume is not direction. A huge-volume day can be heavy selling as easily as heavy buying. That is why our plan reads how the edge bar closed. On a down close, its stop flips to the bar's high, the short side's line.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: Our trims sit at 3R and 5R. What is 1R?
choices: Your risk per share, entry to stop
questions.answer: Your risk per share, entry to stop
questions.why: Your risk per share, entry to stop. Tharp's example: buy at $50 with the exit at $40, and 1R is $10. Our 3R and 5R trims count in those units.
questions.lesson_line: 1R is your risk per share. The targets count up in those units.

wrong.1% of your account: That's an account-risk number. R is per share: the gap from your entry to your stop.
wrong.The first profit target: That's 3R in our plan, the first trim. 1R is the unit the trims are measured in.
wrong.A 1% move in the stock: R isn't a percent move. It's the dollars per share between entry and stop.

questions.lesson_line: 5R: five times your risk per share, on top of the entry.
questions.simple: $52.50, because 5R is five times your risk from the $45.00 trigger to the $43.50 stop, added to the trigger.

deeper.trap: One slip is adding five times the risk to the stop instead of the trigger. That lands one R short of the real target. Always start the count from the trigger.

questions.story: A strong stock with a rising 20-day opens under yesterday's close and sweeps yesterday's low. The day's range is $48.00 to $50.00. It closes at $48.60.
questions.q: Is this a Go Signal day?
choices: No: it closed 30% up its range
Yes: weak open, then a sweep
No: the open was too weak
questions.answer: No: it closed 30% up its range
questions.why: No. A Go Signal day closes in the upper 40% of its range. The range is $48.00 to $50.00, and $48.60 is only 30% of the way up. That is the lower part of the range, nowhere near the top 40%. The weak open, the sweep and the rising 20-day all pass, but the close fails.
questions.lesson_line: No strong close, no Go Signal. The close has to land in the top 40% of the range.

wrong.Yes: weak open, then a sweep: Those are two of the checks. The close must also sit in the top 40% of the range, and 30% doesn't.
wrong.Yes: the 20-day is rising: That's the first check, not the last. A close 30% up the range fails the strong-close check.
wrong.No: the open was too weak: Opening under the prior close is one of the checks, not a flaw. The close is what fails here.

questions.simple: No, because it closed only 30% of the way up its range, and a Go Signal day must close in the top 40%.

deeper.trap: Read 'the upper 40%' from the top of the range down, not from the bottom up. A close 30% of the way up is not inside the top 40%. It sits in the lower part of the range.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact
a computed key
a house plan rule (TRADE_PLANS.md) the owner reviews next

questions.story: Four stocks open under yesterday's close, sweep yesterday's low and close near their highs. A's 20-day average is falling, and C's is flat. B and D have a rising 20-day and ran 15% in five sessions: B two weeks ago, D three months ago. D has had no gap or tight base since.
questions.q: Which one fits our Go Signal?
questions.why: Stock B. Our Go Signal needs a rising 20-day average and a notable recent move. One such move is a 13% gain over 5 sessions within the last 20. B's 15% run two weeks ago fits both. A's 20-day is falling and C's is flat. D's 20-day is rising, but its run was three months ago, with no gap or tight base since.
questions.lesson_line: Go Signal: strength first, then the weak open and the turn.

wrong.Stock C: A flat 20-day fails the rising-average check.
wrong.Stock D: D's 20-day is rising, but its 15% run was three months ago. A run like that has to come within the last 20 sessions.

questions.simple: Stock B, because only B has both a rising 20-day average and a big run inside the last 20 sessions.

deeper.trap: All four stocks show the same weak open, sweep and close near the highs. The day alone cannot pick the Go Signal. What separates them is what came before: a rising 20-day average and a recent run.

reasons: a house plan rule (TRADE_PLANS.md) the owner reviews next

questions.story: A Go Signal day. The stock opens under yesterday's $25.00 close, sweeps support, and buyers turn it. It closes strong at $24.90, never trading $25.00.
questions.q: Where is our entry?
choices: Skip it: no red to green

Here the stock never traded $25.00, so the fallback applies, and the stop is the session's low. Red to green is the first choice, not a must, so this is no reason to skip.

wrong.Today's weak open: The weak open comes before the turn. We don't buy the weakness.
wrong.Skip it: no red to green: Red to green is the first entry, not a must. The plan falls back to the close.

questions.story: VRNS opened 37% down on a gap and closed at the low. A short's obvious stop, the gap day's high, sat 25% over the close.
questions.q: Why does our lesson study this fall instead of shorting it?

Gap downs fill, so it bounces
It closed low, so it's done
Volume was too light to trust
questions.answer: The honest stop is far too wide
questions.why: The honest stop is far too wide. The Bear gap's obvious stop, the gap day's high, sat 25% over the close, so no trade was invented. Our rule: the size comes from the stop, and if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. The lesson shows the line a close must stay under and measures the fall. We do short; this stop just did not fit.

wrong.Gap downs fill, so it bounces: Whether the gap fills isn't the reason. The lesson skips the trade because the stop is 25% away.
wrong.It closed low, so it's done: That isn't the reason. The lesson still measures the fall. The problem is the 25% stop.
wrong.Volume was too light to trust: The story says nothing about volume. The lesson skips the trade because its stop sat 25% away.

questions.simple: The honest stop was 25% away, far too wide for a trade, so the lesson studies the fall instead.

deeper.trap: A big fall looks like an easy short. But the size comes from the stop, so a stop 25% away shrinks the position the rule allows. When the honest stop does not fit the risk, there is no trade, however obvious the move looked.

questions.q: In Bulkowski's tests, how often did the bullish kicking candle reverse the trend?
choices: Barely more than a coin flip
questions.answer: Barely more than a coin flip
questions.why: Barely more than a coin flip. Bulkowski found the bullish kicking candle reversed the trend 53% of the time, which he calls almost random. It is also rare, ranking 100th of 103 candle types by how often it shows up. Investopedia calls kickers rare but highly reliable; Bulkowski's numbers say otherwise. Rare is not the same as reliable.
questions.lesson_line: A candle's name isn't an edge. The plan around it is.

wrong.A reversal almost every time: That's the kicker's reputation, and Investopedia calls it highly reliable. Bulkowski's tests found 53%.
wrong.Almost never a reversal: Not that either. 53% is about even.
wrong.In about 100 of 103 tests: That mixes up a rank with a rate. It ranks 100th of 103 candle types by how often it shows up. It reversed 53% of the time.

questions.simple: It reversed the trend only 53% of the time, barely better than a coin flip, so the name alone is no edge.

deeper.counter: Two good sources disagree. Investopedia calls kickers rare but highly reliable. Bulkowski tested the bullish kicking candle, found 53%, called it almost random, and says not to guess the breakout direction from it. That is why our Kicker comes with a full plan: entry, stop, trims and a trail.

reasons: a tested number the author can revise (53%)
fixed before

Widen it to give the trade room
Leave it where it is and wait for 3R
Raise it to breakeven, your entry

wrong.Widen it to give the trade room: Widening adds risk to a trade that isn't working.

questions.lesson_line: An old gap that holds on the pullback: Gap Support.

A short entry at that high

Yes: it closed in the upper half
No: the dip went too deep

Sell the whole position at the first pop
Hold the full size until the stop hits
Move the stop down to give it room

The higher of the gap top and day's low
The closer of the gap top and day's low
A few cents under the prior day's close

questions.lesson_line: Gap Support stop: the lower of the gap top and the day's low.

Kicker: the textbook shape is narrower than our detector.
